title: A King Asks the Wrong God
overview: When an injured king of Israel seeks answers from a foreign god, Elijah announces his death, and the king's attempts to arrest the prophet end in fire.

parts.label: Moab breaks away (v. 1)
parts.note: Moab, a kingdom east of the Dead Sea, had paid yearly tribute to Israel and now stopped. An ancient Moabite inscription, the Mesha Stone, also boasts of this break, and the story picks up again in chapter 3.

parts.label: A fall and a foreign god (vv. 2-4)
parts.note: Ahab's son Ahaziah, now king, is badly hurt in a fall at home and sends to ask Baal-Zebub, god of the Philistine city of Ekron, whether he will live. Seeking another god broke Israel's most basic law, so the LORD sends Elijah to ask whether the king thinks Israel has no God, and to answer him plainly: he will die.

parts.label: The man in the hair coat (vv. 5-8)
parts.note: The messengers don't know who stopped them, but his rough hair cloak and leather belt, the plain dress of a prophet, tell the king at once that it was Elijah. Christians later noticed that John the Baptist dressed the same way and read him as a new Elijah.

parts.label: Fire on the soldiers (vv. 9-12)
parts.note: The king sends a captain with fifty soldiers to order Elijah down, and the text says fire from heaven killed them all, then did the same to a second captain and his fifty. The story presents this as God defending his prophet against a king who tried to command him, yet the deaths of two captains and their hundred soldiers, men acting under orders, have long troubled readers.

parts.label: A captain who pleads (vv. 13-16)
parts.note: The third captain kneels and begs for his men's lives instead of giving orders, and God tells Elijah to go with him without fear. Elijah then repeats the same verdict to the king's face.

parts.label: The king dies (vv. 17-18)
parts.note: Ahaziah dies with no son, so his brother Joram becomes king. A king with nearly the same name, Jehoram, also ruled Judah at this time, and the dates given here are hard to fit together even for scholars.

disagreement: Christians differ on whether the fire on the soldiers should be read as a just judgment that stands as it is, or as an older picture of God's power that Jesus deliberately set aside when he refused his followers' wish to call down fire on a village (Luke 9).
think: When something frightening happens, like a serious injury, where do you find yourself turning for answers, and what makes that source feel trustworthy to you?
